Tutorial

This page is a guided Angular tutorial for building one complete feature with from the ground up. You will move step by step from project setup, to Feature State definition, to registration and initialization, and finally to a working UI that reads managed State.

By the end of the page, you will have a typed , an Angular service that owns the Feature boundary, a component that binds to reactive State, and a focused detail view that renders a single character from a managed collection.

Business Use Case
  • A product team needs a simple detail view that presents one record from a managed collection without exposing state-management mechanics in the component.
  • The feature must keep domain ownership in a service so UI code can stay focused on display logic, template binding, and user interaction.
  • The same structure should scale from a read-only detail screen to later workflows such as editing, validation, loading states, and testing without changing the core boundary.

Step 2: Install
↑ top

Install the /angular package to add the Angular integration to your project. The package installs the core runtime and exposes the Angular providers, decorator, injector, and Signal-based State access used throughout this tutorial.

The Angular integration includes:

  • provideVault configures the application-level .
  • provideFeatureCell registers a with Angular dependency injection.
  • @ associates an Angular service with its registered .
  • injectVault provides the registered to its Angular service.
  • state (StateSnapshotShape) exposes Signal-based access to the current State:
    • this.vault.state.value()
    • this.vault.state.error()
    • this.vault.state.isLoading()
    • this.vault.state.hasValue()

Step 3: Define Feature State
↑ top

State is the feature-owned data that describes a feature at a specific moment. Defining State means deciding which values belong to the feature, assigning a type to each value, and identifying which properties are required.

In TypeScript, an interface captures those decisions as a compile-time contract for the FeatureCell and its consumers. This contract makes the expected State shape explicit, keeps State usage consistent, and allows TypeScript to identify missing properties and incompatible values during development. The interface defines the shape of State; it does not create or load a State value.

In , each declares State for a single Feature. This keeps the State definition focused on the data owned by that Feature instead of combining unrelated application data into one shared global store definition.

In this tutorial, the Feature and the State represents characters from the Star Wars universe.

Each character has an identifier, name, faction, and force-sensitive status. Keeping these fields in one focused State definition gives the , Pipeline, and Angular application a consistent representation of the character data.

Take Action
  1. Create a new file named: star-wars-character.shape.ts 
{{ starWarsCharacterStateSource.source }}
Global Store vs.

In a global store, all application data is combined into one shared State definition. This can lead to a large, complex State shape that is difficult to manage and maintain. In contrast, a defines State for a single Feature, keeping the State definition focused and manageable.

Step 7: Connect the Service to
↑ top

This is the step where the plain Angular service becomes an SDuX Feature service. The goal is straightforward: connect ExampleService to the registered so the service owns access to the typed feature State.

SDuX adds three pieces here: the @FeatureCell() decorator to associate the service with its key, injectVault() to access the typed FeatureCell API, and initialize() to activate the FeatureCell at runtime.

After this step, the component will no longer need to know anything about FeatureCell registration or initialization. It will read from the service's exposed state, while the service remains the only place that talks directly to SDuX.

Take Action
  1. Create the example.service.ts in the same directory as the State definition.
  2. Decorate ExampleService with the star-wars-character key.
  3. Inject the for readonly StarWarsCharacter[].
  4. Expose the reactive state property from the service.
  5. Call initialize() in the constructor.

Step 8: Display Character State
↑ top

This step narrows the tutorial to the UI-facing files that complete the first read path. The service boundary is already in place; now the component, template, and stylesheet turn that registered character collection into a visible detail view.

For SDuX, the important separation is simple: the component reads display-ready State, and the service owns the FeatureCell.

In this example, the component reads the service's reactive State, derives one displayed character, and passes only template-ready values to the view. The stylesheet is included here because later tutorial expansions reuse the same presentation base.

Step 11: Add a Dropdown
↑ top

This step upgrades the initial SDuX read path from showing the first committed record automatically to letting the user choose which committed record to inspect. The Feature registration, service-owned , and managed collection stay the same; only the UI-facing selection logic changes.

Assume the Angular mechanics are already familiar. The SDuX lesson here is narrower: keep Feature State in the service, keep selection state in the component, and derive the displayed record from the latest service-owned collection. To do that, replace the single displayed-character computed Signal with a read-only character collection, a selectedCharacterId Signal, a computed lookup for the selected record, and a small selection handler. In the template, add a select element that lists the registered characters and keep the detail panel bound to computed controller state instead of reaching into SDuX directly. The verification for this step belongs alongside that delta: the updated component spec should prove the controller starts empty, accepts a valid selection, ignores unknown ids, and renders the selected record without moving SDuX ownership out of the service.

Take Action
  1. Open example.component.ts.
  2. Expose the committed collection and add Signals for the selected character id and selected character.
  3. Add a method that maps the dropdown value to a known character id from the current SDuX-managed collection.
  4. Open example.component.html.
  5. Add a dropdown above the details panel and render an empty state until the user selects a character from the managed collection.
  6. Update example.component.spec.ts to verify both the empty state and the selected-record state.
What to Look For
  • The service still owns the and does not change for this UI enhancement.
  • The selection Signal is presentation state owned by the component, not SDuX Feature State owned by the service.
  • The template continues to render computed, display-ready values instead of reading FeatureCell APIs directly.
  • The spec verifies the new UI behavior without changing the SDuX-owned Feature State contract.

Step 12: Complete Dropdown Tutorial
↑ top

The dropdown tutorial is complete once the page starts with no selected character, lists the registered collection in the picker, and updates the detail panel when the selection changes. The SDuX boundary has not moved: the service still owns the FeatureCell and the component still owns only UI selection state.

This is the smallest useful SDuX expansion of the initial tutorial: the application moves from one fixed read path to one user-directed read path without changing FeatureCell registration, service ownership, or application bootstrap structure. What changed is the proof that the same service-owned State can now support both an initial empty state and a selected-record view.

Take Action
  1. Return to the running Angular application.
  2. Confirm the details panel shows the empty state before a character is selected.
  3. Open the dropdown, choose a character, and confirm the details panel updates to the selected record.
  4. Choose a different character to verify the same read path reacts to the new selection.
What Changed From the Initial Example
  • The component now reads the full collection instead of assuming the first item is always the displayed record.
  • The selected character is derived from a local UI Signal and the latest reactive collection State.
  • The template now teaches user-directed selection on top of the same service-owned State.

Step 13: Add the Add/Edit Service Slice
↑ top

This step turns the user-directed read example into the first mutation slice. The SDuX lesson is still the same: the service owns the , while the component owns only temporary editor state. What changes now is the write path. The service gains the create and update methods that mutate the registered collection, and a small domain helper keeps ID assignment and draft creation out of the Angular service body.

Assume the Angular form primitives are already familiar. Focus on the SDuX boundary: the service assigns IDs, routes creates through mergeState(), routes updates through replaceState(), and keeps every SDuX write inside the service instead of spreading mutation logic across the component and template.

Take Action
  1. Update example.service.ts to add the create and update methods.
  2. Keep the service as the only place that calls SDuX mutation APIs.
Why This Helper Exists

Create example.character-domain.ts to hold the draft type, next-ID helper, and character factory used by this add/edit slice.

This file exists only to keep the service minimal so the tutorial can focus on SDuX teaching principles instead of helper logic.

What to Look For
  • The service owns the write path just as completely as it owned the read path.
  • Create uses mergeState() because it appends a new record to the existing collection.
  • Update uses replaceState() because it replaces one existing record by identity.
  • The domain helper supports add/edit mechanics, but it does not own any SDuX behavior. The service still owns the FeatureCell.

Step 14: Complete Add/Edit Tutorial
↑ top

The add/edit tutorial is complete once the page can enter create mode, validate editor input, save a new character into the managed collection, and reopen an existing character for updates without moving Feature ownership out of the service. The collection picker, detail panel, and form now all react to the same SDuX-managed collection.

This is the first full CRUD-style expansion that still keeps the tutorial disciplined. The component gains form state, mode state, and feedback state, but the service remains the only place that creates or replaces Feature State. That is the important SDuX boundary to preserve before a later destructive-action step adds deletion.

Take Action
  1. Update example.component.ts to add the form, editor mode, feedback state, and save/cancel flows.
  2. Update example.component.html to add the editor panel, the add action, and the empty-state guidance for create mode.
  3. Return to the running Angular application and verify that you can add a character, select it, edit it, and see the detail panel react to the saved State.
Why This Helper Exists

Create example.character-editor.ts to hold the shared validation, normalization, and feedback rules for the add/edit flow.

This file exists only to keep the component minimal so the tutorial can focus on SDuX teaching principles instead of helper logic.

What Changed From the Dropdown Example
  • The component now owns local editor state in addition to local selection state.
  • The template adds a form and feedback region, but it still does not call SDuX APIs directly.
  • Saving a new record and saving an edited record both flow through the same service-owned FeatureCell.
  • Delete is still intentionally absent so this slice can focus on non-destructive mutation only.
